decisions.evidence: Two affixes share this shape. In verb stems ra- is the portative (Parks GO p.44 Table 15 slot 4: ri-, ra-, ruu- PORT; literal translations use 'take', 'carry', 'holding'). In nouns built on a verb (ra+caaka.wi+hus 'the one that sticks out') it is the absolutive mode prefix (GO p.34 Table 8 ra- ABS). The label is chosen by the word class of the headword; Parks prints PORT 4 times and ABS 3 times.
decisions.label: ABS/PORT

decisions.evidence: Parks, Grammatical Overview p.44 Table 15 slot 1 (raar-, ka- ITER) and p.30 Table 4 (-raar- PL on body-part nouns). Parks himself labels raar as PL, ITER or PL/ITER in 68 etymologies; where he prints no label the piece is counted as the same affix. An occurrence with its own lexical gloss in the literal translation stays lexical. Where the literal translation names a sibling or 'planted', the piece is a lexical homonym and is left lexical.
decisions.label: PL/ITER

decisions.evidence: Parks prints DIST for waa in 16 etymologies (e.g. waa+waapic 'flash + DIST'); headword braces give {dist., ...} forms built with -waa-. An occurrence Parks glosses lexically ('hill') stays lexical. Where the literal translation says 'hill', 'mound' or 'growing', the piece is one of the lexical homonyms and is left lexical (the blind re-derivation found 15 such etymologies).
decisions.label: DIST

decisions.evidence: Parks GO p.44: 'locative verbs take the suffix -wi'; Parks prints LOC for wi in 3 etymologies and writes it as the last element of locative stems (kita.wi 'be on top', kaa.wi). His one lexical gloss, 'upright', is kept for the occurrence where he prints it. Where Parks's literal translation says 'upright' or 'vertical', the piece is his lexical wi 'upright' and is left lexical (the blind re-derivation found 29 such etymologies).
decisions.label: LOC

decisions.evidence: One morpheme: Parks GO p.44 Table 15 slot 8 lists -raʔuk as the causative, and the standalone entry raʔuk is glossed 'make'. Parks's literal translations alternate 'make X' and 'cause to be X' for the same piece.

Parks glosses the same piece in the same construction now 'big' and now 'large', even with the same first root: caahikskucuuʔ <icaahiks+kucuu, large person> and caahikstahkucuuʔ <icaahiks+raar+kucuu, big people>. Found by the adversarial pass (the two glosses share no word, so the automatic clustering kept them apart).
Parks glosses the same compound both ways: kiirahkata <kiir+rahkataar, yellow water> and kiirahkataaruʔ <kiir+rahkataar+uʔ, yellow liquid + NOM>. Found by the adversarial pass.

Parks glosses the same piece 'hide' and 'skin' for the same thing, the covering of a tipi: akarahkata <akaar+rahkataar, yellow hide cover> and akahta, literal 'tipi skin to be suspended'. The blind re-derivation records them as one sense; the automatic clustering kept them apart because the two English words share no stem.
